title: South Africa’s offshore-wind pathway links energy security to local jobs, ports, skills, and coastal legitimacy
source_unit: World Bank ESMAP, A Strategic Framework for Offshore Wind Development in South Africa
geography: South Africa’s Exclusive Economic Zone, coastal provinces, ports, grid, supply chains, workers, fishers, maritime users, and communities

observations.period: South Africa offshore-wind development scenarios through 2050

denominator.unit: low, medium, and high offshore-wind growth scenarios

technical_potential.value: the report estimates approximately 95 GW of indicative technical offshore-wind potential in selected suitable regions, mostly associated with floating technology

high_growth.value: the high-growth scenario reaches 1 GW by 2035, 8 GW by 2040, and 40 GW by 2050, roughly 26% of South Africa’s total electricity demand

emissions.value: high-growth deployment could reduce electricity-generation emissions by 530 MtCO2 by 2050; the low-growth scenario could reduce 141 MtCO2

mechanism.value: offshore wind is framed as an energy-security, industrialisation, and just-transition choice rather than only a generation technology

observations.method: Scenario analysis using geospatial resource assessment, electricity-demand and system analysis, cost modeling, grid and port assessment, supply-chain analysis, stakeholder engagement, and socio-economic evaluation.
observations.uncertainty: These are scenarios and indicative technical potential, not a procurement commitment, capacity allocation, investment guarantee, affordability result, or forecast; realization depends on policy, grid, finance, environmental approval, and market conditions.
observations.subgroup: Households and industrial users needing reliable electricity, coastal provinces, energy workers, ports, investors, fishers, maritime users, tourism operators, and communities affected by development.
observations.counterinterpretation: Large-scale deployment can create infrastructure, cost, biodiversity, and community conflicts; lower growth may limit those burdens but also forgo jobs, learning, supply-chain development, and emissions reductions.

observations.period: South Africa offshore-wind jobs, local supply chain, and manufacturing through 2050

jobs.value: large-scale offshore-wind development could support more than 300,000 full-time-equivalent job years between 2030 and 2050

wages.value: associated employment wage contribution could reach US$6.7 billion by 2050

medium_growth.value: the medium scenario reaches 15 GW by 2050, with more than 100,000 local direct FTE job years and US$2.4 billion in employment wage contribution
medium_growth.unit: gigawatts, FTE years, and US dollars

localisation.value: economic benefits scale with deployment and local supply-chain participation, especially manufacturing of floating balance-of-plant components near ports and special economic zones

observations.method: Supply-chain capability assessment and scenario-based direct employment and wage modeling across planning, procurement, manufacturing, transport, installation, operations, maintenance, and decommissioning.
observations.uncertainty: FTE years are not unique people or permanent jobs; the report notes that indirect and induced effects are not fully counted, local capacity is limited initially, and manufacturing assumptions depend on scale, policy, investment, and skills.
observations.subgroup: Workers in energy, manufacturing, ports, logistics, engineering, construction, operations, maintenance, and decommissioning; firms, OEMs, training providers, and coastal provinces.
observations.counterinterpretation: Local-content requirements can support domestic value capture but may raise costs, reduce competition, or slow deployment if they exceed local capability; imported components can lower near-term cost while limiting local learning.

observations.period: South Africa offshore-wind just-transition governance and stakeholder legitimacy

stakeholder_scope.value: the study used multiple engagement rounds with industry developers, national and provincial government, statutory bodies, civil society, think tanks, fishers, maritime users, tourism operators, and communities

justice.value: the report distinguishes procedural, distributive, and restorative justice as requirements for social license and a just transition

enablers.value: long-term strategy, skills development, balanced local-content rules, firm capability, marine spatial planning, leasing, consenting, grid connection, procurement, and health-and-safety processes are identified as enabling conditions

legitimacy_mechanism.value: energy-transition legitimacy depends on whether affected communities can participate meaningfully and whether gains, burdens, and past disadvantages are addressed rather than assumed away

observations.method: Stakeholder engagement, regulatory and permitting review, marine and biodiversity screening, just-transition analysis, and institutional recommendations linked to the three growth scenarios.
observations.uncertainty: Consultation demonstrates an engagement process, not agreement, power-sharing, compensation, or realized community benefit; the report does not establish how stakeholder input changes final siting or investment decisions.
observations.subgroup: Coastal communities, small-scale and commercial fishers, shipping, tourism, conservation groups, workers, municipalities, provinces, national agencies, developers, and electricity users.
observations.counterinterpretation: Early consultation can identify conflicts but may not resolve distributional trade-offs; broad stakeholder inclusion without decision rights or benefit mechanisms can generate participation fatigue and distrust.

boundary: This record adds an energy-transition-to-jobs-and-legitimacy mechanism. It is scenario-based strategic analysis, not proof that offshore wind will be affordable, built, locally owned, job-creating, emissions-reducing, or socially accepted; technical potential, FTE years, wage contribution, and stakeholder engagement must be tested against procurement, finance, grid, environmental, labor, and community outcomes.
